summary: Describes Secure HTTP, a way to protect messages sent over HTTP with confidentiality, authenticity and integrity, and non-repudiation. It is historic; most of the web later used TLS instead.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2660 describes how to protect a single HTTP message rather than the whole connection. The message is wrapped in a secure envelope, and extra headers on both sides say which algorithms and protections are wanted. Each transaction can negotiate its own settings, so a client and a server that disagree simply try again with different options.

subtitle: A way to sign, encrypt and authenticate individual HTTP messages, with the security options negotiated per transaction.

tldr.problem: Many web applications need the client and the server to prove who they are and to exchange sensitive information, but HTTP offered only modest support for cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: S-HTTP wraps each HTTP message in an envelope, adds headers that state which cryptographic options the sender used, and lets both sides state in advance what they will and will not accept.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the message syntax, the option negotiation, the keying headers and a set of error codes for asking a client to retry with different security. It is Historic and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC.

today: RFC 2660 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in August 1999 as an Experimental protocol that protects individual HTTP messages with a secure wrapper and a set of negotiation headers.

sections.title: What Secure HTTP Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
The World Wide Web is a distributed hypermedia system whose native protocol between clients and servers is HTTP. The ease of use of the Web has made it a client/server architecture for many applications, and many of those applications need the client and the server to authenticate each other and exchange sensitive information confidentially. The original HTTP specification had only modest support for the cryptographic mechanisms such transactions need.

S-HTTP is a secure, message-oriented protocol designed to work alongside HTTP. Its design intent is a flexible protocol that supports several operation modes, key management mechanisms, trust models, cryptographic algorithms and encapsulation formats, chosen by option negotiation between the two parties for each transaction. It treats requests and replies symmetrically, giving both sides the same say in their preferences, and it coexists with HTTP's messaging model so that it can be dropped into existing applications.

S-HTTP does not require public key certificates on the client side, because it supports operation with symmetric keys alone. That matters, because it means a spontaneous private transaction can happen between two people who have never met and neither of whom holds a published key. S-HTTP can also make use of an existing certification infrastructure, but does not depend on one. It supports end-to-end secure transactions, where the original HTTP authorization model required the client to try the access first and be refused before any security mechanism came into play. A client can be primed to start a secure transaction from information in the message headers, which is what makes it possible to encrypt the contents of a fill-out form, so that no sensitive data need travel in the clear.

The RFC distinguishes S-HTTP from HTTP's Digest Authentication. S-HTTP adds public key cryptography, and with it digital signatures, as well as confidentiality. This version, S-HTTP/1.4, adds support for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), the successor to PKCS-7, and with it the Diffie-Hellman and the NIST Digital Signature Standard cryptosystems.
sections.plainLanguage: The web needed a way to protect a single request or reply: to prove who sent it, to hide its contents, and to prove nobody altered it on the way. S-HTTP does that inside the message itself, and lets the two ends agree on how each exchange should be protected before it starts.

sections.title: Three Axes of Message Protection
sections.content:
Message protection runs on three independent axes: signature, authentication and encryption. Any message may be signed, authenticated, encrypted, any combination of these, or none at all.

With the signature enhancement, an appropriate certificate may either be attached to the message, possibly along with a certificate chain, or the sender may expect the recipient to obtain the required certificate independently. For bulk encryption S-HTTP defines two key transfer mechanisms. In the first, the symmetric key is passed encrypted under the receiver's public key. In the second, the content is encrypted with a session key that both sides arranged beforehand, and the key identification information is given on one of the header lines. That second arrangement is what lets a confidential message be sent to someone who has no public key pair.

The authentication enhancement verifies message integrity and sender authenticity with a Message Authentication Code, a keyed hash over the document computed with a shared secret. It needs neither public key cryptography nor encryption. The RFC gives it as a lighter mechanism for the many cases where parties need to identify each other reliably in a transaction but do not need third-party non-repudiation, and it notes that signing a transaction should be something the user does consciously, while access control can be met with a lighter mechanism that keeps the scalability advantages of public key cryptography for key exchange.

For freshness, the protocol provides a simple challenge-response mechanism so both parties can be sure that a transmission is current. The integrity protection given to HTTP headers also lets an implementation treat the HTTP Date: header as a freshness indicator, although that requires making allowances for clock skew between the parties, which the RFC says it chooses not to specify.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can be protected in three separate ways, and any of them can be left out. A signature shows who sent it and that nobody changed it. Encryption hides the contents from anyone in the middle. A shared-secret code proves the message came from the other party without needing certificates.

sections.title: The S-HTTP Message Format
sections.content:
Syntactically an S-HTTP message is the same as an HTTP message: a request or status line, then headers, then a body. What differs is that the range of headers is different and the body is typically cryptographically enhanced. The request line uses the special Secure method and the protocol designator Secure-HTTP/1.4, for example Secure * Secure-HTTP/1.4. The request URI is set to an asterisk so that no potentially sensitive information leaks in the clear, and because the method and the designator differ from plain HTTP, S-HTTP and HTTP processing can be mixed on the same TCP port, such as port 80. When a proxy is involved the request URI should instead be the absolute URI with the path replaced by an asterisk.

Responses use the same designator, for example Secure-HTTP/1.4 200 OK. The status in that line says nothing about whether the wrapped HTTP request succeeded: a server should always answer 200 OK provided the S-HTTP processing itself worked, so that an observer cannot tell from the status line whether the request succeeded or failed. The correct recipient learns the answer from the encapsulated data.

All the header lines except Content-Type and Content-Privacy-Domain are optional, and the body is separated from the header block by two successive CRLFs. The Content-Privacy-Domain header says which encapsulation format the body uses: CMS, the Cryptographic Message Syntax, or MOSS, the MIME object security format defined in RFC 1847 and RFC 1848. When the terminal content is an HTTP message its type is message/http; when it is itself an S-HTTP message the type is application/s-http.

Under CMS, signing uses the SignedData type and encryption either enveloping under EnvelopedData with a public key, or the EncryptedData type with a prearranged session key. A message that is both signed and encrypted is built by creating the SignedData production and encapsulating it in the encryption wrapper. Under MOSS the body is a MIME multipart, using multipart/signed for signed messages and multipart/encrypted for encrypted ones. The RFC adds an implementation note that when one agent both signs and encrypts, the signature should generally be applied before the encryption.

Two headers carry the protection that CMS itself does not provide. MAC-Info carries a Message Authentication Code computed over the encapsulated content from the message text, an optional time stamp to stop replay, and a shared secret. This version introduces a construction derived from RFC 2104 in place of the older one, though the old names are kept for backwards compatibility. Prearranged-Key-Info names a key that was arranged outside the cryptographic format, with two methods: inband, where the key was passed earlier in a Key-Assign header, and outband, where the agents have external access to the key material.
sections.plainLanguage: An S-HTTP message looks like an HTTP message with a different first line and extra headers. The real message is sealed inside a standard envelope format, either CMS or MOSS. Two extra headers carry the protections that those envelope formats do not cover, such as a shared-secret code over the contents.

sections.title: Negotiating Cryptographic Options
sections.content:
Both parties can state what cryptographic enhancements they require, will accept and refuse. A negotiation header is a sequence of specifications, each with four parts: the property being negotiated, such as the bulk encryption algorithm; the value under discussion, such as DES-CBC; the direction affected, namely reception or origination from the originator's point of view; and the strength of preference, which is required, optional or refused. So the line SHTTP-Symmetric-Content-Algorithms: recv-optional=DES-CBC,RC2 can be read as: you are free to use DES-CBC or RC2 to encrypt messages to me.

The syntax is a field followed by key-value pairs, where a key is a mode and an action joined by a hyphen. The mode is either orig or recv, and the action is optional, required or refused. A receiver that marks an enhancement optional will process it if the other party uses it but is also happy to process messages without it. A receiver that marks it required will not process messages without it, and one that marks it refused will not process messages that use it. On the sending side, an optional enhancement is dropped when the other party refuses it and used when the other party requires it; a required enhancement is always produced and a refused one never is. Optional values are listed in decreasing order of preference, and an agent is free to pick any member of the intersection of the two lists, or none.

The headers defined this way cover the privacy domains (CMS and MOSS), certificate types (X.509 and X.509v3), key exchange algorithms (DH, RSA, Outband and Inband), signature algorithms (RSA and NIST-DSS), message digest algorithms, the symmetric ciphers for the content and for the headers, the MAC algorithms, and the privacy enhancements themselves, which are sign, encrypt and auth. A further header, Your-Key-Pattern, says which keys are acceptable for covering, authenticating or signing, using patterns matched against certificate names.

Ciphers with variable key lengths can be parametrized, so RSA[1024] names a 1024-bit key, and a range can be written as a cipher with two bounds. The special value inf means infinite length, and a cipher written with no length at all is read as the maximum range possible with that cipher. The RFC also lists default preferences for every header, which apply unless a key is set explicitly. The defaults are modest: CMS for the privacy domain, X.509 for certificates, DH, Inband and Outband for key exchange, NIST-DSS for signatures, RSA-MD5 for digests, DES-CBC for content, DES-ECB for headers, and for the enhancements an originator may sign, encrypt or authenticate while a receiver must have encryption and may have signing or authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, each side can list what it wants: which algorithms to use, whether the reply must be signed or encrypted, and which certificates are acceptable. Both lists travel with the message, so each side can check that what it got matches what it asked for. Where nothing is said, the RFC supplies a default set of preferences.

sections.title: Keying Material and Freshness
sections.content:
Several headers carry keying material rather than preferences. Encryption-Identity names the principal for whom the message could be encrypted, which explicitly allows the reply to be encrypted under a public key without the other agent having signed first. Certificate-Info carries certificates so that the receiver can perform public key operations on the named identities without fetching them separately; the certificate group may be in PEM format or as a base-64 encoded CMS SignedData message, and several such headers may be present.

Key-Assign binds a key to a symbolic name for later reference. It names the method, the key name, a lifetime and the ciphers the key applies to. The lifetime is this, meaning the key is probably good only for reading this transmission, reply, meaning it is useful for a reply, or unspecified, meaning it may be reused for an indefinite number of transactions. The only method defined is inband, the direct assignment of an uncovered key to a name, given as a hexadecimal string after the semicolon. The RFC calls inband assignment especially important, because it is what allows confidential spontaneous communication between two agents where only one of them holds a key pair, and it is also useful for changing keys without any public key computation. Because the key is unprotected, this header must sit inside the secured request and may not be used in an unencrypted message.

Freshness is handled with nonces. A nonce is an opaque, transient, session-oriented identifier whose value is a local matter and might simply be a random number generated by the originator; its only job is to be returned by the recipient, which echoes it in a Nonce-Echo header inside the encapsulated headers so that the echo is itself cryptographically protected. Several nonces can be supplied and each is echoed independently. A separate header, Security-Scheme, must be generated by every S-HTTP compliant agent in all the HTTP messages it produces, with the value S-HTTP/1.4, so that other agents can detect they are talking to an S-HTTP peer and produce the right option headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers that carry keys say where the key came from, how long it is good for, and which algorithms it may be used with. One kind of key is handed over directly in the message, which is how two people can have a private exchange when only one of them has a key pair. A nonce is a random value sent one way and echoed back, so that both ends can tell the message is current.

sections.title: Retrying and Security Errors
sections.content:
A server may answer with an error code that says the request has not completely failed, only that the client might succeed with a different set of cryptographic options. This happens, for example, when the page holding the link the client followed is old and did not require a signature, but the server now has a policy that requires one for that address. The options the server wants are carried in the header of the encapsulated HTTP message, in the same way the client's own options are carried.

The RFC defines several status codes for this. 420 SecurityRetry tells the client that the current request is rejected but that a retry with different cryptographic enhancements is worth attempting; it is also used when a plain HTTP request arrives where an S-HTTP one was needed. For an S-HTTP request it means the enhancements applied were unsatisfactory, and it can be used to force a new public key negotiation when the session key has expired or to supply a fresh nonce. 421 BogusHeader says something about the request was bad and is followed by an explanation. 422 SHTTP Proxy Authentication Required is the same idea as 420 but for a proxy. 320 SHTTP Not Modified is for proxy interaction: it says the message that follows carries enough keying material for the proxy to forward a cached document to the new requester, with the enhanced content left out and the original transaction key re-covered for the new recipient.

The RFC then warns about automating that retry, because it opens several kinds of attack. Its example is a credit card. The user views a document that needs the card, checks that the name in the certificate is the one they expect and that the request will be encrypted, and follows the link. An attacker intercepts the server's reply and answers with a message encrypted under the client's public key carrying a Moved 301 header; a client that followed the redirect automatically would give away the card. So clients should never re-encrypt data automatically unless the server asking for the retry proves that it already holds the data. That proof is acceptable in three cases: the retry response was encrypted under an inband key freshly generated for the original request, the retry response was signed by the intended recipient, or the original request used an outband key and the response is encrypted under that key. Where automatic re-encryption is not appropriate, the client should ask the user. Automatic retry of the signature enhancement is prohibited outright.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can turn a request away and say which security it would accept instead. The RFC warns that a client should not retry such a request on its own, because an attacker could use the same trick to redirect a payment. The client should ask the user before trying again, and it must never add a signature on its own.

viz.caption: THE FOUR THINGS S-HTTP CAN DO TO A MESSAGE

items.title: Sign
items.text: A digital signature proves who sent the message and that nobody changed it. It needs a certificate, which may travel with the message or be fetched separately.

items.title: Encrypt
items.text: The contents are encrypted, either with a key passed under the receiver's public key or with a session key both sides arranged earlier.

items.title: Authenticate
items.text: A Message Authentication Code computed with a shared secret proves the sender without any public key cryptography.

items.title: Freshness
items.text: A nonce is sent and echoed back, so that both ends can tell the transmission is current rather than replayed.

viz.caption: THE REQUEST LINE, STATUS LINE AND A REPRESENTATIVE HEADER BLOCK FROM THE RFC

data.title: S-HTTP message pieces

items.label: OK
items.desc: The normal answer. It says nothing about whether the wrapped HTTP request succeeded.

items.label: SecurityRetry
items.desc: The request was rejected, but a retry with different cryptographic options is worth attempting.

items.label: BogusHeader
items.desc: Something about the S-HTTP request was bad. The code is followed by an explanation.

items.label: SHTTP Proxy Authentication Required
items.desc: The client must apply the enhancements in the message to satisfy a proxy.

items.label: SHTTP Not Modified
items.desc: The message carries keying material so a proxy can forward a cached document, with the content left out.
